before.content_html:
Britain Before the Longships

By the late eighth century Britain was already a patchwork made by migration. The Anglo-Saxons — themselves descendants of fifth-century settlers from northern Germany and southern Denmark — had divided the land into rival kingdoms: Northumbria, Mercia, East Anglia and Wessex. Christianity, brought by missionaries from Rome and Iona, had given these kingdoms a shared faith but not a shared crown. Coastal monasteries held silver chalices, illuminated gospels and grain stores, and they were defended by little more than prayer.

In 793 a fleet of Norse Vikings sacked Lindisfarne, the great island monastery off Northumbria. The chronicler Alcuin wrote that “never before has such terror appeared in Britain”. The raid is often treated as a Year Zero, but it was the start of a long process: nearly three centuries of arrivals that turned raiders into settlers and reshaped who counted as English.

Key Fact

The Lindisfarne raid of 793 is the conventional starting point for Viking activity in Britain. Alcuin’s shocked account survives because monastic writers were the chief literate witnesses — and the main victims.

Why Did the Vikings Come?

No single cause explains the raids. Population pressure in Scandinavia made younger sons hungry for land; partible inheritance meant farms were carved up too small to support a family. Improvements in shipbuilding produced the shallow-draught longship, which could cross open sea and then row up rivers like the Thames or the Liffey. Trade routes already linked Scandinavia to Frankia and the Baltic, so raiders knew where the rich monasteries were. And the political fragmentation of Britain — competing kings, no standing fleet — made it a soft target.

Religion mattered too. Norse warriors did not share Christian taboos against attacking churches, so undefended monasteries with portable wealth looked less like sacred ground and more like an open vault. The role of individuals also fed the wave: war-leaders such as Ivar the Boneless and Halfdan built reputations on plunder, and reputations attracted followers.

For the first sixty years the Norse came in summer fleets and went home in autumn. From 851 they began wintering on English soil. In 865 the so-called Great Heathen Army landed in East Anglia — not to plunder and leave, but to conquer. Within ten years the Norse had killed or driven out the kings of Northumbria, East Anglia and Mercia. Only Wessex still stood.

Alfred & the Defence of Wessex

In 871 the young king Alfred came to the throne of Wessex with the Great Heathen Army camped on his border. After a string of defeats he was driven into the marshes of Athelney in early 878, hiding from a winter raid led by Guthrum. Later that year he rallied the men of Somerset, Wiltshire and Hampshire and broke the Danes at the Battle of Edington. Guthrum was forced to accept baptism — with Alfred as his godfather — and to withdraw beyond a treaty line.

Alfred did not just win one battle; he changed how Wessex defended itself. He built a network of fortified towns called burhs, redesigned the army so that half could fight while half worked the fields, and ordered the construction of larger ships. He also commissioned learning: scholars translated key Latin works into Old English, and the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle began to record the year-by-year story of his kingdom. By his death in 899 he was the only Anglo-Saxon king ever called ‘the Great’.

The Danelaw

Edington did not expel the Norse. The peace negotiated with Guthrum, refined under Alfred’s son Edward and his daughter Aethelflaed, formalised a division of the country. North and east of a line running roughly from London to Chester became the Danelaw: an area where Danish custom, language and units of land measurement (the wapentake, the carucate) prevailed. South and west remained Anglo-Saxon under West Saxon kingship. The boundary did not freeze identities; it created a permeable frontier across which traders, marriages and Christian missionaries moved freely.

Within two generations Norse settlers in the Danelaw were buying land, attending English law courts and christening their children with hybrid names. Place names tell the story: villages ending in ‘-by’ (Whitby, Grimsby), ‘-thorpe’ (Scunthorpe) or ‘-toft’ mark Norse settlement, while words like ‘sky’, ‘egg’, ‘law’ and ‘them’ entered everyday English. The legal pronoun ‘they’ is a small daily reminder that the country’s grammar is itself the product of migration.

Guthrum’s baptism in 878 began a religious shift that ran the wrong way round to most modern assumptions: the conquerors converted to the religion of the conquered. By the early tenth century Norse settlers were endowing churches, minting coins with crosses, and being buried in Christian cemeteries. Religion thus became a glue holding the two populations together rather than a wedge driving them apart — an important corrective to the idea that medieval English identity was ever ‘pure’ Anglo-Saxon.

Key Fact

The Danelaw was carved out by treaty after Edington (878). It was a permeable frontier, not a wall — place-name evidence (Whitby, Grimsby, Scunthorpe) shows Norse settlement persisted long after the boundary itself faded.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of the creation of the Danelaw for the development of Britain.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two or three developed points of significance, addressing both significance at the time and significance over time, with precise factual support (Edington 878, Guthrum’s baptism, place-name evidence, Norse loanwords).
Secure: Two clear points of significance with relevant detail; some sense of long-term legacy.
Developing: Significance described rather than explained; mostly short-term consequences.
Emerging: Generalised statements about Vikings without focused significance.

Indicative content:
• At the time: the Danelaw stabilised a frontier after years of raids, allowing Wessex and the Danish-settled north to coexist and trade.
• At the time: it formalised a legal and cultural divide (wapentakes, carucates) that shaped land law for centuries.
• Over time: place names ending in -by, -thorpe and -toft mark the area to this day; everyday English words such as sky, egg, law, them are Norse in origin.
• Over time: the Christianisation of the Danes after Guthrum’s baptism set a pattern of integration rather than expulsion that recurs across the unit.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of the Lindisfarne raid of 793.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Developed points addressing the raid’s short-term shock and its longer-term place in shaping Britain’s relationship with Scandinavia, with precise detail (Alcuin, monastic wealth, opening of three centuries of Viking activity).
Secure: Two clear points of significance with detail.
Developing: Recounts the raid without explaining wider significance.
Emerging: General statements about Viking violence.

Indicative content:
• At the time: a wealthy, undefended Christian monastery was attacked, exposing the vulnerability of the Anglo-Saxon kingdoms’ coastlines.
• At the time: Alcuin’s letters and chronicles preserved the event, shaping the way contemporaries saw the Norse threat.
• Over time: the raid is the conventional opening of nearly three centuries of Norse arrivals that produced the Danelaw, the North Sea Empire and ultimately the Norman Conquest.
• Over time: it warns against treating 1948 (Windrush) as the start of migration to Britain — large-scale arrivals were already shaping the country a thousand years earlier.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of the Christianisation of the Danes for British identity.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Developed significance points addressing both immediate religious change and the longer pattern of integration, with precise detail (Guthrum’s baptism 878, Norse-built churches, hybrid place names).
Secure: Two clear points of significance with detail.
Developing: Describes conversion without explaining significance.
Emerging: General statement about religion.

Indicative content:
• At the time: Guthrum’s baptism in 878 turned the Danelaw boundary from a religious as well as political frontier into a shared Christian world.
• At the time: shared Christianity made intermarriage and shared law enforcement easier, easing the integration of Norse settlers.
• Over time: it set a pattern for Britain in which incoming groups (Normans, Huguenots, later Irish Catholics) integrated rather than being expelled.
• Over time: it complicates the modern claim that British identity is ‘Christian’ in some pure Anglo-Saxon sense — the Christianity that prevailed was already shared with the Norse newcomers.

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways in which Viking arrivals in Britain in the ninth century were similar to or different from later migrations to Britain (such as the Huguenots in the seventeenth century).
practice_questions.type: 4 marks — Two Ways Similar or Different
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two clearly distinct similarities or differences, each supported with precise detail from across the period.
Secure: Two valid points with brief support.
Developing: One clear point; second weak or repetitive.
Emerging: Vague comparison without specific detail.

Indicative content:
• Difference: Vikings arrived as armed raiders and conquerors (Great Heathen Army 865); Huguenots arrived as Protestant refugees (after 1685) seeking asylum, not conquest.
• Similarity: both groups settled and integrated economically — Norse settlers farmed and traded across the Danelaw; Huguenots brought silk-weaving and finance to London.
• Similarity: both left a lasting linguistic footprint — Norse vocabulary in everyday English; French-derived terms in textiles and finance.
• Difference: the Vikings imposed their own legal system in part of the country (Danelaw); Huguenots adapted to existing English law and church structures.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle for our understanding of this period.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Developed significance points addressing both contemporary purpose and long-term influence on the historical record, with precise detail (begun in Wessex in the 890s, multiple copies, continued to 1154).
Secure: Two clear points with detail.
Developing: Describes the Chronicle without explaining significance.
Emerging: Vague statement about written history.

Indicative content:
• At the time: the Chronicle gave Alfred’s court a written record of West Saxon achievement, useful for political legitimacy.
• At the time: it spread to monastic centres outside Wessex, creating the first sustained narrative of an English-speaking people.
• Over time: it remains the chief contemporary source for the Viking Age in Britain — without it, our knowledge of Edington, the Danelaw and the Norse rulers would be much thinner.
• Over time: its preservation shapes the questions historians can ask — the Norse perspective survives mainly through the eyes of the people they fought.

lessons.title: Cnut, Emma & the North Sea Empire

before.content_html:
A Second Wave of Vikings

Alfred’s descendants reconquered the Danelaw in the early tenth century, and by 927 Athelstan ruled a single kingdom of England for the first time. But the Norse were not finished. From the 980s a second wave of raids battered the country under King Aethelred, ‘the Unready’ (more accurately ‘ill-counselled’). Aethelred tried to buy peace by paying a vast tribute called the Danegeld, raised by a heavy land tax. The strategy failed: each payment encouraged a fresh fleet to come back for more.

In 1002 Aethelred ordered the St Brice’s Day massacre of Danes living in his kingdom — an episode the spec’s longer view treats as a warning about how host populations have responded to migrants. The killings provoked the Danish king Sweyn Forkbeard, whose sister was reportedly among the dead, to launch a full-scale invasion. By the time Sweyn died in 1014 his son Cnut was poised to claim the English throne, and after a short war Cnut became king of England in 1016.

Key Fact

Aethelred’s 1002 St Brice’s Day massacre of Danes living in England helped trigger Sweyn Forkbeard’s invasion. Within fourteen years Sweyn’s son Cnut was crowned king of England.

Cnut’s Rule

Cnut ruled England from 1016 to 1035, and after 1018 also Denmark, and from 1028 also Norway. Together these territories made up what historians call the North Sea Empire. It was not an empire in the modern sense; there were no shared institutions, only the same king. But it tied England into a Scandinavian world of trade, marriage and military networks for two decades.

Cnut governed England through Anglo-Saxon laws and English-speaking earls. He confirmed the laws of King Edgar, gave generous endowments to English monasteries, and went on pilgrimage to Rome in 1027. The famous story of Cnut commanding the tide to retreat is a later fiction, invented to show that he knew — against the courtiers’ flattery — that no king is above God. He cultivated, in other words, the public image of a Christian English king, not a foreign conqueror, while keeping Danish housecarls as his personal guard.

A personal union meant the kingdoms shared a king but kept their own laws, churches and government. England remained governed in English; Denmark in Danish. The arrangement was fragile because it depended on one life. When Cnut died in 1035 his sons Harold Harefoot and Harthacnut squabbled, and the empire fell apart within seven years.

Emma of Normandy

The figure who held this Scandinavian-English-Norman world together was a queen, not a king. Emma of Normandy was the daughter of Duke Richard I of Normandy. She married Aethelred in 1002 to seal an Anglo-Norman alliance against Viking raids. After Aethelred’s death she married his Danish conqueror Cnut in 1017 to seal another alliance — this time between the new Danish king and the existing English political class.

Emma was the mother of two future English kings — Edward the Confessor (Aethelred’s son) and Harthacnut (Cnut’s son) — and the great-aunt of William the Conqueror. Her unique position as queen of two rival dynasties commissioned the Encomium Emmae Reginae, a piece of political writing designed to justify her family’s claim to the throne. She is a rare medieval figure who chose to write — or commission — her own version of events.

The 1066 Succession Crisis

Cnut’s sons died young. The throne returned in 1042 to Emma’s English son Edward the Confessor, who had spent his exile at the Norman court. Edward died childless in January 1066, and the question of who should rule England produced four rival claimants: Harold Godwinson (the leading English earl), Edgar Aetheling (the last male of the West Saxon line), Harald Hardrada of Norway (claiming through Cnut’s son Magnus), and William of Normandy (claiming through Edward’s mother Emma and a disputed promise).

The succession crisis was, in part, the legacy of Cnut’s North Sea Empire and Emma’s two marriages: each of the four claimants traced his case through the Scandinavian-English-Norman links forged in this generation. The events of 1066 — the battles of Fulford, Stamford Bridge and Hastings — closed one period of cross-Channel kingship and opened another.

From the Lindisfarne raid in 793 to the death of Harthacnut in 1042, Britain was repeatedly remade by Norse arrivals. Cnut’s reign is the high point: a Danish king ruling through Anglo-Saxon institutions, married to a Norman noblewoman, while his housecarls stood guard. The picture is messier than ‘Vikings raided Britain’ — by the eleventh century the rulers of England were Vikings, and English government, language and Christianity carried on around them.

Key Fact

Emma of Normandy linked three royal houses. Married first to Aethelred and then to Cnut, she was the mother of Edward the Confessor and Harthacnut and the great-aunt of William the Conqueror. The 1066 crisis grew directly out of these family ties.
before.exam_tip_html: For the 4-mark Two Ways Similar or Different question, give exactly two ways and ground each one in concrete detail. A common error is to write three vague ways instead of two precise ones. Strong answers might compare Viking arrivals before 878 (raid-then-leave) with Cnut’s rule (settle and govern through existing institutions) — the same Norse origin, but two very different relationships with English authority.

before.content_html:
From Conquest to Cross-Channel Realm

William of Normandy’s victory at Hastings on 14 October 1066 ended the Anglo-Saxon dynasty and bolted England onto a French-speaking duchy across the Channel. The Norman elite replaced almost the entire English aristocracy: by 1086, when the Domesday Book was compiled, fewer than ten of England’s 200 leading landholders had English names. The new rulers spoke Norman French, ate French food, built stone castles and brought continental architectural styles that produced Durham Cathedral and the White Tower of London.

For the next 150 years ‘England’ was rarely a free-standing kingdom. The same king ruled both England and Normandy, and most royal courts and battles were on the continental side of the Channel. The Anglo-Saxon Chronicle continued to be written in English — an act of cultural resistance — until the last entry in 1154, by which point the king (Henry II) ruled an even bigger French-language empire.

Key Fact

By the time of Domesday Book in 1086, fewer than ten of England’s top 200 landholders had English names. The Norman Conquest was a near-total replacement of the ruling class, not just a change of king.

Henry II & the Angevin Empire

Henry II became king in 1154. He was not just king of England; he had inherited Normandy, Maine and Anjou from his parents and acquired Aquitaine through marriage to Eleanor in 1152. Together these territories — running from the Cheviots to the Pyrenees — made up the Angevin Empire. It was, like Cnut’s earlier North Sea Empire, a personal union: each region kept its own laws, language and customs, and the king moved constantly between them.

In 1171 Henry took an army to Ireland and forced its high king and major lords to accept him as overlord. The expedition began the long English involvement in Ireland that became one of the most consequential strands of the whole spec — the Ulster Plantations of the seventeenth century, the Famine migration of the 1840s, and the partition of 1921 all flow from decisions taken in this period. The Irish church accepted reform along Roman lines, and Anglo-Norman barons began to settle the eastern Irish coast around the area later called the Pale.

Three motives intersected. First, Pope Adrian IV had earlier issued the bull Laudabiliter, encouraging an English king to reform the Irish church — religion provided cover. Second, Anglo-Norman barons such as Strongbow had already entered Ireland on private invitation; Henry wanted to bring them under royal control before they became independent rivals. Third, the personal union model made expansion easy: Ireland could be added to the king’s portfolio without any change to England’s laws or institutions.

Government on the Move

Ruling an empire that stretched from northern England to the Spanish border meant Henry was almost always travelling. To govern in his absence he expanded the royal exchequer at Westminster, sent justices in eyre on circuits across England, and pushed the use of jury trial. The result was a paradox — a king who spent most of his time in France strengthened the institutions of royal justice in England. The seeds of common law were planted while the throne itself was rarely on English soil.

Henry’s court was multilingual: Norman French for the king and barons, Latin for clergy and government documents, English for the great majority of the population. This three-language stack persisted for two centuries and is the reason modern English vocabulary contains parallel words from each tier — pig (English) and pork (French), house (English) and mansion (French), kingly (English) and royal (French).

King John & the Loss of Normandy

Henry’s sons could not hold the empire together. After Richard I’s death in 1199, John inherited the throne. In 1204 the French king Philip Augustus invaded Normandy and overran it within months. Within five years John had also lost Anjou, Maine and most of Poitou, leaving only Gascony in the south-west and a thin band of England-Channel-Aquitaine connections. The Angevin Empire was effectively over.

The losses had two enormous consequences. First, the king now ruled an island kingdom (plus a small French foothold) for the first time since 1066 — English politics turned inward, and the Norman aristocracy had to choose between their English and Normandy estates, breaking the cross-Channel landholding that had defined the previous 150 years. Second, John’s desperate attempts to fund a war of reconquest through heavy taxation produced a baronial revolt in 1215 and the great charter known as Magna Carta — a document born directly from the unravelling of the Angevin Empire.

The loss of Normandy in 1204 mattered for identity, not just territory. While the king ruled lands on both sides of the Channel, ‘English’ and ‘French’ were not opposites. After 1204 the two crowns ruled separate kingdoms, and over the thirteenth century the English aristocracy began to identify with England rather than with a continental homeland. Lesson 4 will pick up this thread, showing how the Hundred Years’ War turned the rivalry into a forge for English identity.

Key Fact

The loss of Normandy in 1204 ended the cross-Channel realm built by William and Henry II. England turned inward, the Anglo-Norman aristocracy had to choose sides, and John’s tax demands triggered the 1215 baronial revolt that produced Magna Carta.

practice_questions.text: Explain how Anglo-Irish involvement developed from Henry II’s 1171 invasion to the loss of Normandy in 1204.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two or three developed stages with explicit consequences linking them, including precise detail (Strongbow, Laudabiliter bull, the Pale, Anglo-Norman barons, John’s position).
Secure: Clear sequence of stages with some causal links.
Developing: Mostly narrative; consequences thin.
Emerging: General statement about Ireland.

Indicative content:
• Stage 1: Anglo-Norman barons such as Strongbow entered Ireland on private invitation in 1169-70, threatening to set up an independent power.
• Stage 2: Henry II’s 1171 expedition brought these barons under royal control and forced Irish kings to accept him as overlord.
• Stage 3: Anglo-Norman settlement spread along the eastern coast, the area later known as the Pale, while the Irish church was reformed along Roman lines.
• Stage 4: under John, attention turned to defending Normandy; Ireland was already governed at one remove by royal officials, a pattern that survived the loss of Normandy and shaped centuries of Anglo-Irish relations.

lessons.title: The Hundred Years' War & English Identity

before.content_html:
A War of More Than a Hundred Years

The struggle remembered as the Hundred Years’ War was not really one war or one hundred years. It was a sequence of campaigns and truces fought between 1337 and 1453, sparked when the French king Philip VI confiscated English-held Gascony and the English king Edward III responded by claiming the French throne through his mother, Isabella of France. The war is normally divided into three phases: the Edwardian (1337-1360), the Caroline (1369-1389) and the Lancastrian (1415-1453).

For our thematic study the names of battles matter less than what the war did to the kingdoms that fought it. Crécy (1346), Poitiers (1356) and Agincourt (1415) showed that an English king could win pitched battles deep inside France using the longbow and disciplined infantry. Joan of Arc’s relief of Orleans in 1429 turned the tide; by 1453, when the French recaptured Bordeaux, every continental possession except Calais had been lost.

Key Fact

The Hundred Years’ War ran from 1337 to 1453. Crécy (1346), Poitiers (1356) and Agincourt (1415) gave England moments of dominance, but by 1453 only Calais remained of England’s once vast French territories.

The Rise of English

For nearly three centuries after 1066, English had been the language of the marketplace and the home but not of the elite. The Hundred Years’ War accelerated a switch already under way. From 1362 the Statute of Pleading required cases in English courts to be argued in English. From the same year, parliaments were opened in English. By the early fifteenth century Geoffrey Chaucer’s Canterbury Tales (c1387) had shown that serious literature could be written in the vernacular. Henry V (1413-22) used English in his official letters — the first king since 1066 to do so consistently.

War with France made it politically awkward to keep speaking French at court. The barons whose grandfathers had been Norman were now being sent into battle in the name of an ‘English’ king against a ‘French’ enemy. Identity hardened along the language line. By 1453 ‘Englishness’ was a coherent idea in a way it had not been at the war’s start — a clear example of how war as a factor produced cultural change far beyond the battlefield.

The court’s switch to English did not erase French and Latin overnight. Latin remained the language of church, university and high government records into the seventeenth century. French survived in legal vocabulary (parliament, court, justice) and in the formal language of the royal household (the still-used ‘la reyne le veult’ that signals royal assent in modern legislation). What changed was the centre of cultural gravity: by Henry V’s reign the king of England spoke and wrote in English to his subjects.

Parliament’s Growing Role

War cost money. Edward III and Henry V could only sustain campaigns abroad if they could tax England at home, and from the 1340s only Parliament could authorise the taxes. Each grant gave the Commons a chance to demand reform — redress of grievances before supply, in the phrase of the time. The Good Parliament of 1376 impeached royal ministers; the so-called Wonderful Parliament of 1386 humiliated Richard II. Parliament thus became a permanent feature of government, not because kings welcomed it but because they could not pay for the war without it.

The institution that emerged was specifically English: a Lords and Commons that met at Westminster, debated in English by the late fourteenth century, and passed statutes binding on all the king’s English subjects. The institutional idea of England as a single political community was strengthened every time Parliament voted a war tax.

Loss of Empire, Birth of a Kingdom

The collapse of the continental empire after 1450 looks like failure, but it had a curious side-effect: England became more itself. The same kings who had owned land in Normandy, Aquitaine and Anjou now had to rule a smaller, island-and-Calais kingdom from Westminster. The Anglo-Irish lordship inherited from Henry II remained, but the focus shifted definitively to English politics, the English Channel, and an English-speaking court.

A second consequence followed quickly. With no continental wars to fight and no French territory to govern, the great noble families turned on each other. The Wars of the Roses (1455-1487) between the houses of York and Lancaster were partly a hangover from the Hundred Years’ War — military families with no foreign enemy turned to civil war. Out of that conflict came the Tudors, the Reformation, and the early-modern empire-building covered in the rest of this unit.

The end of the war removed England’s continental option. Looking outward now meant looking across the open Atlantic, not across the Channel. Within a hundred years of Bordeaux’s fall in 1453, English ships under John Hawkins (covered in Lesson 6) were trading enslaved Africans across to the Caribbean, and Walter Raleigh (Lesson 7) was promoting a colony at Roanoke. The end of one empire helped open the door to another, very different one.

Key Fact

The Hundred Years’ War accelerated three changes inside England: English replaced French at court (1362 onwards), Parliament became indispensable for war taxation, and a sharper sense of Englishness emerged in opposition to a foreign enemy.

lessons.title: Medieval Migrants: Hanseatic Merchants, Jews & Lombards

before.content_html:
Britain Was Never Just Anglo-Saxon

Between the Norman Conquest and the end of the Hundred Years’ War, Britain was tied into a network of European trade and finance that pulled in merchants, bankers and craftsmen from far beyond its shores. Three groups stand out: the medieval Jewish communities invited in by William the Conqueror, the German Hanseatic League merchants who ran the London Steelyard, and the Italian (especially Lombard) bankers of Lombard Street. None of these communities is named in a single spec bullet, but the spec opens in c790 and the question of who came to Britain in the medieval period sits between Part 1 (Conquered and Conquerors) and Part 2 (Looking West). Knowing these groups gives you ready-made comparisons for the 4-mark question.

Key Fact

William the Conqueror invited Jews to England from Rouen around 1070; Edward I expelled them in 1290 with the Edict of Expulsion. The community lasted in England for around 220 years before becoming the first European Jewish population to be formally banished by royal decree.

Medieval Jews in England, c1070-1290

After 1066, William brought Jewish merchants and moneylenders from Rouen to provide credit for the Norman elite. Christian doctrine forbade Christians from charging interest on loans (usury), but the new Norman state needed cash to build castles, fund crusades and run government. Jewish lenders filled that gap. Communities grew in London, York, Lincoln, Norwich and Oxford. Jews were technically the king’s personal property — the Crown taxed them heavily and could seize their property at will.

This protection was fragile. The 1190 York Massacre, in which around 150 Jews died after taking refuge in Clifford’s Tower, showed that royal protection collapsed under crusade-era anti-Jewish violence. By the 1270s Edward I had already taxed Jewish wealth past the point of usefulness, and richer Italian bankers were arriving from the south. The 1290 Edict of Expulsion ordered every Jew out of England by All Saints’ Day. Around 2,000-3,000 left. England was officially without a Jewish community for 366 years, until Cromwell quietly readmitted them in 1656.

The first recorded blood libel in Europe — the false accusation that Jews killed Christian children for ritual purposes — was the case of William of Norwich in 1144. The libel spread from England to the rest of Christian Europe and was used to justify centuries of violence. The 1255 case of Hugh of Lincoln saw 19 Jews hanged on the same charge despite no evidence; Henry III seized their property. By the time of the 1290 expulsion, English Jewish communities had been pauperised by royal taxation and brutalised by mob violence. The story of medieval English Jews is therefore not a story of comfortable migration but of conditional toleration that finally turned to expulsion.

The Hanseatic Merchants and the London Steelyard

Across the same period, German merchants from Lübeck, Hamburg, Cologne, Danzig and other Baltic and North Sea ports formed the Hanseatic League. From the 1200s they operated the Steelyard, a walled compound on the north bank of the Thames near modern Cannon Street station. They imported timber, wax, fur, grain, pitch and tar from the Baltic and exported English wool and (later) finished cloth. The Steelyard had its own warehouse, dormitory, chapel and even rules — resident merchants were celibate while they lived there.

English kings granted the Hanseatic merchants generous privileges — lower tolls than English merchants paid, freedom from many local taxes — in return for credit and guaranteed supply of Baltic goods. By the fifteenth century English merchants resented this. Hostility built up across the sixteenth century: in 1597 Elizabeth I revoked the league’s privileges and expelled the merchants from the Steelyard. The site was kept by the Crown and eventually demolished in the nineteenth century to build Cannon Street station.

Lombard Bankers and Italian Finance

From the late 1200s, Italian bankers — especially from Lucca, Florence and Genoa — replaced the Jewish moneylenders Edward I had expelled. They were Christian, so the usury ban was a problem, but they invented techniques (bills of exchange, partnerships, complicated currency-conversion contracts) that worked around it. The London street where their counting-houses clustered is still called Lombard Street; the symbol of their guild, three golden balls, became the modern pawnshop sign.

The Italians financed Edward III’s opening campaigns of the Hundred Years’ War. When the king defaulted on his debts in 1340, two of the great Florentine banking houses — the Bardi and Peruzzi — collapsed. The crash devastated Florentine finance and left a long memory of English royal unreliability. By the fifteenth century, English merchant banks were starting to take over from the Italians, but the techniques (and Lombard Street itself) stayed.

For the 4-mark comparison question, these three medieval migrations give you sharp contrasts. Jews were brought in by William the Conqueror specifically as moneylenders and were expelled when the Crown no longer needed them — their position depended on royal economic interest. The Hanseatic merchants were not invited but tolerated for the goods and credit they brought; Elizabeth I expelled them when their privileges had become politically embarrassing. Italian bankers came as private operators chasing royal-debt profits and stayed because their techniques outlasted the families who first practised them. All three groups show the same pattern: medieval kings used migrants when economic resources demanded it, and removed them when politics changed.

Key Fact

Three medieval migrations show three different drivers. Jewish migration into England (c1070-1290) was driven by royal demand for credit. The Hanseatic Steelyard (c1200-1597) was driven by Baltic trade. Italian banking (from c1280) was driven by the gap left after the 1290 expulsion. Each ended when the political mood turned: 1290, 1597 and gradually through the fifteenth century.

before.content_html:
From Piracy to Plantation

English involvement in the Caribbean began with violence at sea. Sixteenth-century privateers such as Francis Drake plundered Spanish silver fleets with royal approval; the line between piracy and state policy was deliberately blurred. John Hawkins took the next step. On three voyages between 1562 and 1567 he attacked Portuguese slave ships off West Africa, sold the captives in Spanish Caribbean ports and returned to England with profit. Elizabeth I knighted him; she also granted him a coat of arms showing a bound African as the crest. From this beginning, England turned a system of piracy into a system of permanent plantation and forced labour.

Key Fact

John Hawkins made the first English slave-trading voyages in 1562-1567. By the late 17th century the Royal African Company (chartered 1672) had built a structured triangular trade: British goods to Africa, enslaved Africans to the Americas, sugar and tobacco back to Britain.

Settling Barbados and the West Indies

The English settled Barbados in 1627. Early colonists tried tobacco and cotton; neither paid. By the 1640s Dutch advisers had introduced sugar cane from Brazil. Sugar was hugely profitable but extraordinarily labour-intensive: cane needed to be cut, crushed and boiled within hours of harvest, in tropical heat, year after year. Indentured English servants and Irish convicts could not provide the volume or endure the conditions. Planters turned to enslaved Africans. By 1700 Barbados had around 50,000 enslaved people on 800 plantations — the most densely enslaved population in the British world. Jamaica, captured from Spain in 1655, scaled the same model up. By 1750 Britain held Barbados, Jamaica, the Leeward Islands, Antigua and St Kitts — the ‘Sugar Islands’ that drove imperial wealth.

The Triangular Trade and the Middle Passage

From the 1670s the Royal African Company ran a state-backed monopoly on the African trade. After Parliament opened the trade to private merchants in 1698, Liverpool and Bristol overtook London. Liverpool ships carried around 1.5 million enslaved Africans across the Atlantic between 1700 and 1807 — more than any other port in the world. The Middle Passage — the second leg of the triangle — killed around one in seven captives in transit; chained into hold space the size of coffins, with foul food, no sanitation, and outbreaks of dysentery and smallpox. Across the whole Atlantic trade, around 12.5 million Africans were forcibly transported and at least 1.8 million died on the voyages.

These are not abstract figures. Olaudah Equiano’s autobiography (1789) describes the ‘loathsomeness of the stench’ aboard a slave ship and the children ‘suffocated’ in the hold — the kind of testimony abolitionists would use to change British public opinion.

Liverpool grew from a small port of around 5,000 in 1700 to nearly 80,000 a century later, with profits ploughed into wet docks (1715), insurance, banking and ship-building. Bristol’s Queen Square and Clifton terraces, Glasgow’s Tobacco Lord mansions and London’s West India Dock (1802) all carried slave-trade money. Country estates — Harewood House in Yorkshire, Penrhyn Castle in Wales, Dodington Park in Gloucestershire — were built or expanded on Caribbean plantation profits. The 2013 Legacies of British Slave-ownership database (UCL) lists more than 46,000 individual slave-owners compensated under the 1837 settlement — ordinary people, not just aristocrats, had a stake in the system.

Economic Impact on Britain

Sugar, tobacco and cotton flowed back to Britain in vast quantities. By 1750 the Caribbean was responsible for around 40% of Britain’s long-distance trade. Slave-trade profit funded marine insurance (Lloyd’s of London), banking (Barclays, Heywood’s Bank in Liverpool), and the early industrial revolution — James Watt’s improved steam engine of 1769 was developed in a Glasgow funded heavily by slave-derived sugar and tobacco wealth. Historians disagree on how decisive this contribution was: Eric Williams’s 1944 Capitalism and Slavery argued it was central; later historians have shown the picture is more complex. But no serious account of eighteenth-century British wealth can leave slavery out.

The Social Impact and the Abolition Movement

Slavery shaped British culture as much as British commerce. Sugar in tea, tobacco in pipes, mahogany in furniture and printed cotton on walls all came from slave economies. So did the Black presence in Britain itself: by the 1770s around 10,000-15,000 Black people lived in Britain, many of them servants in wealthy households, some free, some still legally enslaved. The 1772 Somerset case — in which Lord Mansfield ruled that an enslaved man, James Somerset, could not be forcibly removed from England — was widely (mis)understood as having abolished slavery on English soil.

From the 1780s a sustained abolitionist movement built up around Thomas Clarkson, William Wilberforce, the formerly enslaved writers Olaudah Equiano and Ottobah Cugoano, the Quakers, and the Sons of Africa society. Their work combined eyewitness testimony, statistical research (Clarkson’s plan of the slave ship Brookes), parliamentary lobbying and consumer boycotts of West Indian sugar. The 1791 Haitian Revolution — an enslaved uprising that overthrew French colonial rule — showed that abolition could come from the enslaved themselves. Parliament abolished the slave trade in 1807 and slavery itself in the British Empire in 1833. The 1833 act paid £20 million in compensation — not to the formerly enslaved, but to the slave-owners.

The British abolition movement was not led only by white reformers. The Sons of Africa, formed around 1787, was a society of formerly enslaved Africans living in London — Olaudah Equiano, Ottobah Cugoano and others — who lectured, signed petitions and wrote letters to the press. Cugoano’s 1787 Thoughts and Sentiments on the Evil of Slavery was the first abolitionist work published by an African in Britain. Equiano’s 1789 autobiography sold so many copies that he became wealthy enough to leave money to his daughter; he toured Britain raising support for abolition. Their work shows abolition was an Atlantic movement, not a British gift.

Key Fact

The Slave Trade Act of 1807 ended the British slave trade; the Slavery Abolition Act of 1833 ended slavery throughout most of the British Empire. Around 12.5 million Africans had been forcibly transported across the Atlantic; at least 1.8 million died during the Middle Passage.

Weighing the Factors

For a 16-mark factor essay, the slave trade is a textbook case of economic resources as a driver of empire — sugar, tobacco and cotton wealth funded ports, banks, country houses and (some of) the industrial revolution. But economic factors did not act alone. Ideas — first racial hierarchies justifying slavery, then Christian and Enlightenment arguments against it — shaped both the trade and its abolition. The role of individuals mattered on both sides: Hawkins began the trade, Wilberforce and Clarkson helped end it, and Equiano showed that abolition was an Atlantic movement, not a British gift. The strongest essays show how these factors interacted rather than ranking them mechanically.

• Role of individuals: Hawkins (1562-67), Wilberforce, Clarkson, Equiano, Cugoano — both sides of the abolition struggle had named figures whose actions mattered.
• Government: chartered the Royal African Company; passed the 1807 Slave Trade Act and 1833 Slavery Abolition Act; the £20 million compensation went to owners not the enslaved.
• War: the 1791 Haitian Revolution and the wars of the French Revolution undermined the Caribbean plantation system and created the strategic conditions for British abolition.

before.content_html:
Looking West After 1453

When the Hundred Years’ War ended in 1453, Englishmen who had thought of empire as a stretch of land across the Channel had to look elsewhere. Over the next 200 years, looking west — first to the Caribbean (Lesson 6) and then across the Atlantic to mainland North America — came to define a new English ambition. Walter Raleigh launched the first attempt at Roanoke (1585); Jamestown (1607) was the first permanent settlement; the Mayflower’s Pilgrim Fathers (1620) added a religious dimension; and over the next century and a half thirteen British colonies stretched along the Atlantic coast. The story ends with the loss of those colonies in 1783 — a defeat that paradoxically pushed Britain towards the very different empire of nineteenth-century India and Africa.

Key Fact

Sir Walter Raleigh promoted the failed Roanoke colony in 1585. Jamestown, founded by the Virginia Company in 1607, was the first permanent English settlement in North America. The Mayflower’s Pilgrim Fathers reached Plymouth in 1620.

Raleigh and Roanoke: A False Start

Sir Walter Raleigh never set foot on the colony he sponsored. In 1585 he fitted out an expedition under his cousin Sir Richard Grenville to settle Roanoke Island (in modern North Carolina). Three years of supply problems, hostile relations with local Algonquian peoples and the diversion of English shipping into the 1588 Armada war left the colony abandoned. The 1590 supply mission found the settlement empty, with the word CROATOAN carved into a post — the so-called ‘lost colony’ mystery. Raleigh’s pattern of enthusiasm without follow-through would be repeated in dozens of early English Atlantic ventures.

Jamestown 1607: The First Permanent Colony

In 1607 the Virginia Company sent 105 men to a marshy peninsula on the James River. Two-thirds were dead within a year, mostly from dysentery, malaria and starvation. The colony only survived because of the leadership of John Smith, the corn supplied (and sometimes withheld) by the Powhatan Confederacy under Wahunsenacawh, and the introduction of tobacco by John Rolfe around 1614. Tobacco changed everything. By the 1620s Virginia had a profitable export crop, and the colony shifted from a quasi-military outpost into a plantation society. The 1619 arrival of around 20 Africans from a Portuguese slave ship at Point Comfort marks the first recorded enslaved African presence in English North America — the long shadow of the trade that would define the southern colonies.

Most early settlers were not enslaved Africans — they were indentured servants from England, Scotland and Ireland. Around 200,000 indentured servants crossed the Atlantic in the 17th century. They signed contracts (indentures) committing them to four to seven years of unpaid labour in exchange for their passage. About four in ten died before completing their term. Survivors received a small grant of land and a few tools at the end — the so-called ‘freedom dues’. As tobacco profits rose and African slavery scaled up, planters increasingly preferred enslaved labour, which came with no contract and no end-date. By 1700, indentured servitude was in decline; chattel slavery had taken its place.

The Pilgrim Fathers: Religion as a Push Factor

The 1620 voyage of the Mayflower brought a different kind of migrant. Around 35 of the 102 passengers were Separatists — Puritan dissenters who had already fled to Leiden in the Netherlands and now hoped to build a godly community in the New World. The Pilgrim Fathers signed the Mayflower Compact, agreeing to govern themselves by majority vote — an early model of self-government in the colonies. The early winter at Plymouth killed half the settlers, but the colony survived on supplies provided by the Wampanoag people under Massasoit. Larger Puritan migration followed: the 1630 ‘Great Migration’ brought around 20,000 Puritans to Massachusetts under John Winthrop, who promised a ‘city upon a hill’. Religion was the dominant push factor for New England in a way it never was for Virginia.

Contact with Indigenous Peoples

English settlement was only possible because of Indigenous knowledge — the Powhatan in Virginia, the Wampanoag and Massachusett in New England. Settlers learned to plant maize, dig clams and tap maple sap from people whose ancestors had farmed the same land for thousands of years. Relations broke down quickly. Smallpox, measles and influenza, brought by Europeans, killed an estimated 90% of the Indigenous population of the Atlantic seaboard between 1500 and 1700 — one of the worst demographic catastrophes in human history. The 1622 Powhatan rising killed around 350 settlers; the English response wiped out Powhatan villages and seized their land. King Philip’s War (1675-76), led by the Wampanoag chief Metacom against the New England colonies, killed around 800 settlers and at least 3,000 Indigenous people, ending most Indigenous resistance east of the Connecticut River.

The Loss of America, 1763-1783

By 1763 the British had won the Seven Years’ War against France and gained Canada. London tried to cover the war debt by taxing the thirteen American colonies (Stamp Act 1765, Townshend duties 1767, Tea Act 1773). Colonists who had grown used to almost a century of light-touch ‘salutary neglect’ called the new taxes tyranny. The 1773 Boston Tea Party, in which colonists tipped East India Company tea into Boston Harbour, hardened British policy. Fighting broke out at Lexington and Concord in April 1775. The 4 July 1776 Declaration of Independence committed the colonies to break with Britain. After French intervention from 1778 the British surrendered at Yorktown in 1781; the 1783 Treaty of Paris recognised the United States. Britain had lost thirteen colonies, around two million colonists and the most populous part of its empire.

The defeat in 1783 looks like the end of empire, but it was not. With the United States lost, British attention shifted to Asia (the East India Company, Lesson 9), Australia (claimed 1788, partly to dump convicts now that the American colonies would no longer take them), and eventually Africa (Lesson 10). The ‘second British Empire’ of 1783-1914 was very different from the first — less about white settlement, more about commerce and military rule over non-white populations. The 1783 defeat also produced the Black Loyalists: around 3,000 formerly enslaved people who had fought for the British in exchange for freedom, and were resettled in Nova Scotia and (later) Sierra Leone — an early example of empire reshaping the British Black population.

Key Fact

The Boston Tea Party (1773), Declaration of Independence (1776) and Treaty of Paris (1783) marked the loss of the thirteen American colonies. Britain’s response was to push the ‘second empire’ into India, Australia and (later) Africa.
before.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Raleigh’s 1585 Roanoke failure preceded Jamestown’s 1607 success; tobacco from c1614 turned Virginia from outpost to plantation economy.
  • The Pilgrim Fathers (1620) and the 1630 Great Migration brought 20,000 religious dissenters to New England, embedding religion as a colonial push factor.
  • Disease and warfare killed around 90% of the Atlantic-coast Indigenous population by 1700; the 1773-1783 American Revolution lost Britain its largest settler empire and pushed it east towards India and Africa.

lessons.title: Migrants In & Out: Huguenots, Highland Clearances & Ulster

before.content_html:
Three Movements, Three Motives

Between roughly 1600 and 1850, three very different migrations reshaped Britain and Ireland: French Protestant Huguenot refugees fleeing Catholic France, Lowland Scots and English settlers planted into Ulster, and Highland Scots driven off their land by their own clan chiefs. Each was driven by a different mix of religion, government policy and economic resources. Together they show that British migration history before Windrush is not a single story — people moved in, out and within Britain for very different reasons.

Key Fact

In 1685 Louis XIV revoked the Edict of Nantes, which had protected French Protestants. Around 50,000 Huguenots fled to Britain in the years that followed, settling mainly in Spitalfields, London, Canterbury and Norwich.

Huguenots: Religion as Push, Skills as Pull

Huguenots had been a tolerated Protestant minority in France since the Edict of Nantes of 1598. When Louis XIV revoked it in 1685, Huguenots faced forced conversion, the destruction of their churches and the kidnapping of their children. Around 200,000 left France in total — roughly 50,000 came to Britain. Charles II and James II issued royal proclamations promising shelter, and Parliament backed this with a 1689 act of naturalisation.

The reception was unusually warm because Huguenots brought useful skills. They settled in Spitalfields in east London and turned it into the centre of British silk weaving. Others built up Canterbury’s and Norwich’s textile trades. Goldsmiths, watchmakers, gunsmiths and bankers (the founders of the Bank of England in 1694 included several Huguenot families) added economic weight. The word ‘refugee’ entered English from this moment — from French réfugié, applied first to the Huguenots.

In 1290 Edward I had expelled the Jewish population of England; in 1597 Elizabeth I expelled the Hanseatic merchants from the London Steelyard. Yet Huguenots in 1685 were welcomed. The difference was a mix of religion and economics: Huguenots were Protestant, like most of the English political class, and were arriving in a kingdom that had just lived through anti-Catholic panics. Their skills also matched a national strategy — English textile manufacturers were trying to compete with French silk and Dutch fine cloth, and the Huguenots brought exactly the techniques needed.

The Ulster Plantation: Government Migration

A century earlier, in 1609, James I had launched the Ulster Plantation: confiscated Catholic Irish land in six counties (Donegal, Tyrone, Tyrconnell, Armagh, Cavan and Fermanagh) was redistributed to around 100,000 Lowland Scots and English Protestant settlers. The aim was political, not economic — the Crown wanted a loyal Protestant population in Ireland to prevent rebellion and Spanish intervention. Settlers received land cheaply on condition that they bring tenants, build defended towns and exclude Catholic Irish from the best holdings.

The plantation succeeded as a population transfer but at the cost of long-term sectarian division. Catholic Irish populations were pushed onto poorer land. The 1641 rising killed thousands of settlers; Cromwell’s 1649-50 reconquest then dispossessed the Catholic Irish even further. By 1700 Ulster had a Protestant Scots-Irish majority that has continued to shape Northern Irish politics ever since.

The Highland Clearances: Forced Out at Home

In the Scottish Highlands between roughly 1750 and 1860, clan chiefs replaced their tenants with sheep. The Highland Clearances were a private, profit-driven migration: the chiefs had become landlords in the British legal sense after the failure of the 1745 Jacobite rising, and Cheviot sheep produced higher rents than Gaelic-speaking smallholders. Tenants were given short notice, their cottages were sometimes burnt down behind them (the Sutherland clearances of 1814 are notorious), and they were pushed to coastal ‘crofting’ townships, to Lowland cities, or onto emigrant ships to North America and Australia.

In May 1814 Patrick Sellar, factor (estate manager) for the Countess of Sutherland, evicted around 1,500 tenants from Strathnaver. Houses were torn down and sometimes burnt while their occupants were still inside; one elderly woman, Margaret McKay, died days later from her injuries. Sellar was tried for culpable homicide in 1816 and acquitted. The case became a touchstone of clearance memory: those who survived it carried Gaelic-language ballads and stories with them to Cape Breton, North Carolina and the Glasgow tenements, keeping the trauma alive across the Atlantic.

Three Migrations, Compared

For the 4-mark ‘two ways similar or different’ question, these three movements give you ready-made comparisons. Religion drove Huguenot flight and shaped the Ulster plantation, but had no role in the clearances — they were economic. Government directed the Ulster plantation explicitly and welcomed the Huguenots through naturalisation, but stayed out of the clearances. Economic resources attracted Huguenots to Spitalfields silk and pushed Highlanders onto emigrant ships, while shaping landlord behaviour in both Ulster and the Highlands. The reception of incomers also differed: Huguenots were welcomed for their skills, planted Ulster Scots were imposed on a hostile native population, and Highland evictees were strangers in their own country.

Key Fact

Huguenot migration was driven mainly by religion (push) and economic resources (pull). The Ulster Plantation was driven mainly by government policy. The Highland Clearances were driven mainly by economic resources — landlord profit from sheep farming.
before.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • After Louis XIV revoked the Edict of Nantes in 1685, around 50,000 Huguenots came to Britain. Their silk weaving, banking and craft skills made Spitalfields, Canterbury and Norwich centres of new manufacturing.
  • The Ulster Plantation of 1609 transferred around 100,000 Scottish and English Protestants onto confiscated Catholic Irish land — a government-engineered migration with long-term sectarian consequences.
  • The Highland Clearances (c1750-1860) cleared Gaelic tenants for Cheviot sheep, sending them to Lowland cities, North America and Australia — an economic migration imposed by their own clan chiefs.

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways in which the experience of Huguenot migrants in the late 17th century was similar to or different from the experience of evictees during the Highland Clearances.
practice_questions.type: 4 marks — Two Ways Similar or Different
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Difference: Huguenots fled religious persecution by a foreign king (Louis XIV); Highland evictees were forced out by their own clan chiefs in the pursuit of profit from sheep farming.
• Difference: Huguenots were welcomed and naturalised by Charles II and James II because their skills were valued; Highland evictees received no government protection and were often turned out without warning.
• Similarity: both groups produced lasting communities far from their place of origin — Huguenot silk weavers in Spitalfields, Highland diaspora in North America and Australia.
• Similarity: both migrations were shaped by economic resources — Huguenot skills attracted them to British towns, Cheviot sheep displaced Highlanders from the glens.

[4 marks — 2 marks per comparison: 1 for a basic point, 2 for a developed point]

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways in which the Ulster Plantation and the Highland Clearances were similar or different.
practice_questions.type: 4 marks — Two Ways Similar or Different
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Difference: the Ulster Plantation was a government-directed migration in which James I confiscated Catholic Irish land for Protestant settlers; the Highland Clearances were private, driven by individual landlords seeking profit from sheep.
• Difference: Ulster settlers were given land they had not previously held; Highland tenants were removed from land their families had farmed for generations.
• Similarity: both involved displacement of an existing population — Catholic Irish in Ulster, Gaelic Highlanders in the glens.
• Similarity: both produced large overseas diasporas — Scots-Irish migration to America from Ulster, Highland migration to Cape Breton, North Carolina and Australia.

[4 marks — 2 marks per comparison: 1 for a basic point, 2 for a developed point]

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of Huguenot migration for Britain in the late 17th and 18th centuries.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• At the time: around 50,000 refugees arrived in a kingdom of around 5 million — one of the largest single migrations in early modern Britain.
• At the time: Spitalfields silk weaving, Canterbury and Norwich textile trades were transformed; Huguenot bankers were founder members of the Bank of England in 1694.
• Over time: the word ‘refugee’ entered English from French; later refugee movements (Jewish 1881, Ugandan Asian 1972) were measured against Huguenot success as a precedent.
• Over time: Huguenot family names (Garrick, Olivier, Bosanquet, Courtauld) became woven into the British establishment, showing how integration could happen across generations.
• Limitation: assimilation took 100+ years; French churches in London survived into the 19th century, showing that integration was gradual rather than immediate.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Sustained significance covering both at the time and over time with precise dates and examples.
Secure: Clear significance with relevant examples covering both periods.
Developing: Significance attempted but uneven.
Emerging: Brief identification only.

practice_questions.text: Explain how the policy of the British government towards migration changed during the period 1600 to 1850.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• In 1609 James I directed migration into Ireland through the Ulster Plantation — an active state policy of confiscation and resettlement.
• In 1685 Charles II issued a royal proclamation welcoming Huguenots; the 1689 Act of Naturalisation enshrined this in law.
• By the 18th century the state took a more passive approach to internal migration: it neither directed nor restricted Highland depopulation, leaving it to landlords.
• The state did intervene in some economic migrations (Bounty schemes for skilled workers; legislation regulating Irish migration into England in famine years).
• Causal chain: from active state-sponsored colonisation (Ulster) to selective welcome of useful refugees (Huguenots) to non-intervention in internal forced movement (Highland Clearances).

[8 marks]
Mastering: Sustained causal development showing change over time with precise examples.
Secure: Clear development with relevant examples.
Developing: Some development; balance uneven.
Emerging: Lists events without causal links.

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways in which religion shaped migration to and from Britain in the early modern period.
practice_questions.type: 4 marks — Two Ways Similar or Different
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Religion as push: Louis XIV’s 1685 revocation of the Edict of Nantes drove around 50,000 Protestant Huguenots out of France; Britain’s Protestant identity made it an obvious refuge.
• Religion as state strategy: the 1609 Ulster Plantation transplanted Protestants from Lowland Scotland and England into Catholic Ireland to secure the kingdom for the Crown.
• Religion as integration helper: shared Protestantism made Huguenot integration into British towns relatively rapid compared to later Catholic Irish migration.
• Religion as exclusion: even welcomed Protestant migrants kept their own French churches; full assimilation took several generations.

[4 marks — 2 marks per comparison: 1 for a basic point, 2 for a developed point]

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of the Highland Clearances for Scotland and the wider British world.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• At the time: tens of thousands of Gaelic-speaking tenants were evicted between c1750 and 1860, ending the traditional clan-tenancy system that had survived the 1745 Jacobite rising.
• At the time: the population of the Highlands fell sharply; coastal crofting townships, Lowland slums and emigrant ships absorbed the displaced.
• Over time: Highland diasporas in Cape Breton (Canada), North Carolina, Australia and New Zealand carried Gaelic language, ballads and clan identity overseas.
• Over time: the clearances became a defining episode in modern Scottish national memory and a touchstone for debates on land ownership and the Crofters’ Holdings (Scotland) Act 1886.
• Limitation: economic migration from rural Scotland would have happened to some extent without the clearances, given the pull of industrial Glasgow.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Sustained significance covering both at the time and over time with precise dates and examples.
Secure: Clear significance with relevant examples.
Developing: Significance attempted but uneven.
Emerging: Brief identification only.

lessons.title: Expansion in India: Company to Crown

before.content_html:
A Company That Became an Empire

The British acquired India almost by accident. In 1600 Elizabeth I granted a royal charter to a group of London merchants — the East India Company — giving them a monopoly on English trade with Asia. For the first 150 years they were one trading company among many, competing with Dutch, French and Portuguese rivals. By 1857 the same company had become the political ruler of an Indian empire of 200 million people, with its own army, courts, currency and tax system. Untangling how this happened — and what it cost both Britain and India — is the spine of the AQA factor essay on empire.

Key Fact

At the Battle of Plassey in 1757, Robert Clive defeated the Nawab of Bengal Siraj ud-Daulah using bribery, betrayal and a small Company army. Plassey gave the East India Company control of Bengal’s tax revenue — the moment a trading company became a territorial power.

Robert Clive and the Battle of Plassey, 1757

Robert Clive arrived in India as a Company clerk in 1744. He showed a soldier’s talent in skirmishes with the French at Arcot (1751) and Calcutta (1757), recapturing the city after the Nawab of Bengal had captured it the previous year (the ‘Black Hole’ of Calcutta). Plassey itself was less a battle than a managed coup: Clive bribed the Nawab’s commander, Mir Jafar, who held back his forces while Clive’s 3,000-strong army faced down 50,000. Mir Jafar was installed as a puppet ruler. The Company received tax revenue from Bengal — the diwani — in 1765, formalising the new arrangement. From this point on, Bengali peasant taxes paid for British armies that conquered the rest of India.

Warren Hastings and Company Rule

Warren Hastings became the first Governor-General of Bengal in 1772. He centralised Company government, reformed the tax system, expanded the Company army (the sepoy regiments) and patronised Indian scholarship — he commissioned the first English translation of the Bhagavad Gita. Yet his methods were ruthless: he extracted huge sums from the Begums of Oudh and the Raja of Benares to pay for war. On his return to Britain in 1785 he was impeached for corruption. The trial dragged on until 1795 when he was acquitted — but the case fixed in British public opinion the idea that Indian rule needed regulation. Pitt’s India Act 1784 had already given Parliament a controlling Board over Company decisions.

Lord Dalhousie, Governor-General from 1848, used the Doctrine of Lapse to annex Indian states whose rulers died without a natural-born male heir. Adopted heirs (a long-standing Hindu practice) were no longer accepted. Satara (1848), Jhansi (1853), Nagpur (1854) and finally Oudh (1856) all ‘lapsed’ to the Company. Annexing Oudh was the spark that lit the powder keg: many sepoys came from Oudh, and now their homeland had been confiscated by the Company they served.

The 1857 Indian Rebellion

In May 1857 sepoys at Meerut shot their British officers and marched on Delhi, where they declared the elderly Mughal emperor Bahadur Shah II the head of a restored empire. The trigger was the greased cartridges for the new Enfield rifle, rumoured to be greased with cow fat (offensive to Hindus, who venerate the cow) and pig fat (offensive to Muslims, who consider the pig unclean). To load the rifle, a sepoy had to bite the cartridge open. The deeper causes were: anger at the Doctrine of Lapse; resentment at evangelical Christian missions; new laws permitting widow remarriage; and the annexation of Oudh.

The rising spread across northern and central India — Lucknow, Cawnpore, Jhansi (where the Rani fought as a cavalry leader). It took the British 14 months to suppress it, helped by Punjabi and Sikh troops who stayed loyal. The reprisals were savage: rebel sepoys were sometimes blown from cannons; whole villages were destroyed. Bahadur Shah was put on trial and exiled to Burma. The Company was dissolved. The Government of India Act 1858 transferred direct rule to the Crown, making Queen Victoria sovereign of India and creating the position of Viceroy. In 1877 Disraeli proclaimed Victoria Empress of India. The British called it the ‘Indian Mutiny’; Indian nationalists later called it the ‘First War of Independence’.

Key Fact

Causes of the 1857 Rebellion included the greased cartridges, the Doctrine of Lapse (especially the annexation of Oudh in 1856), missionary activity and laws seen as attacking Hindu and Muslim custom. The Government of India Act 1858 ended Company rule and put India under direct Crown government.

Impact on Britain and India

Empire reshaped both societies. In Britain, Indian wealth helped fund country houses (Robert Clive’s Powis Castle holds an Indian collection that is still in place today), the Bank of England and the consumer revolution — cotton, tea, sugar, indigo. Indian words entered English: bungalow, pyjamas, shampoo, jodhpurs, verandah. The Company army opened a route to wealth for younger sons of the gentry. In India, the picture is more contested. Britain built railways (53,000 km by 1947), telegraph, postal services, irrigation canals and English-language universities. But it also imposed cash-crop economies that worsened famines (the Bengal famines of 1770 and 1943 each killed millions), restricted Indian industry to protect British exporters, and held political power above all but a handful of Indians until 1947.

Linking to the Factor Essay

India is the keystone case study for the AQA factor essay. Economic resources drove the Company’s expansion: textiles, opium, indigo, tea. War turned trading posts into provinces — Plassey, the Mysore wars, the Maratha wars, the Sikh wars, the 1857 reprisals. Ideas justified British rule: from Hastings’ orientalism to Macaulay’s 1835 Minute on Education arguing for English-language schooling. The role of individuals is unavoidable — Clive, Hastings, Dalhousie, the Rani of Jhansi. A 16-mark essay on India needs to weigh which of these factors did the heaviest work, and the strongest answers note that economic resources and war reinforced each other: tax revenue paid for armies, armies seized more revenue.

practice_questions.text: ‘Economic resources were the most important factor in British expansion in India between 1757 and 1857.’ To what extent do you agree? Use examples drawn from across the period in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Students should weigh economic resources against at least two other factors (war, ideas, role of individuals, government) with a substantiated overall judgement.

In support of economic resources as the main factor:
• The East India Company was a trading company; its drive into India followed cotton, opium and tea profits.
• The 1765 Bengal *diwani* gave the Company tax revenue that funded its armies; one province paid for the conquest of others.
• British industrial demand for cotton and Indian markets for British manufactures made empire commercially self-sustaining.

Weighed against war:
• Plassey 1757, the Mysore wars (1767-99), the Maratha wars and the Sikh wars repeatedly turned trading posts into provinces.
• The 1857 reprisals showed that without superior military force the Company could not hold India.

Weighed against the role of individuals:
• Clive’s personal generalship at Plassey, Hastings’ political consolidation, Dalhousie’s Doctrine of Lapse and the Rani of Jhansi’s resistance all shaped events that economic forces alone do not explain.

Weighed against ideas:
• Macaulay’s 1835 Minute on Education and evangelical missionary activity provided ideological justification; Indian responses to evangelism helped trigger 1857.

Judgement: Economic resources drove expansion but war secured it — the two reinforced each other. Individuals decided pace; ideas decided how empire was administered. The strongest answers reach across the period to compare 1757 (private corporation profit) with 1858 (state-led empire).

[16 marks plus 4 SPaG]
Mastering: Sustained complex argument weighing the named factor against at least two others with examples from across the period and a substantiated overall judgement.
Secure: Clear analysis with comparison and judgement.
Developing: Lists factors without consistent comparative judgement.
Emerging: Describes economic causes only, or fails to weigh factors.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of the Battle of Plassey (1757) for the development of British rule in India.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• At the time: Clive’s victory installed a puppet Nawab (Mir Jafar) and gave the East India Company effective control of Bengal.
• At the time: the 1765 grant of *diwani* turned military victory into permanent tax revenue from one of India’s richest provinces.
• Over time: Bengali tax revenue funded the Company army that conquered the rest of India over the following century.
• Over time: Plassey is conventionally treated as the start of British India — the moment a trading company became a territorial empire.
• Limitation: the Company would still have needed Hastings’ later consolidation to turn military victory into a workable government.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Sustained significance covering both at the time and over time with precise dates and examples.
Secure: Clear significance with relevant examples.
Developing: Significance attempted but uneven.
Emerging: Brief identification only.

practice_questions.text: Explain how British control of India developed between 1757 and 1858.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:

• 1765: the *diwani* grant turned military success into permanent tax revenue.
• 1772: Warren Hastings became first Governor-General; centralised Company rule and expanded the sepoy army.
• 1784: Pitt’s India Act gave Parliament a Board of Control; the state began to oversee the Company.
• 1848-56: Lord Dalhousie used the Doctrine of Lapse to annex Indian states without natural heirs (Satara, Jhansi, Nagpur, Oudh).
• 1857-58: Indian Rebellion; the Government of India Act 1858 dissolved the Company and put India under direct Crown rule.
• Causal chain: trading post → tax-collecting territory → expansionist Company → rebellion → direct empire.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Sustained causal development with precise examples covering at least four stages.
Secure: Clear development with relevant examples.
Developing: Some development; balance uneven.
Emerging: Lists events without causal links.

practice_questions.text: Explain two effects of the 1857 Indian Rebellion.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Effect on government: the Government of India Act 1858 abolished the East India Company and transferred rule to the Crown; in 1877 Victoria became Empress of India.
• Effect on government: a new Viceroy and India Office in London replaced Company governance, giving Parliament direct control.
• Effect on Indian society: British post-1858 policy avoided overt cultural reform — missionary activity was restricted, princely states’ adoptions were respected.
• Effect on memory: the rebellion became a long-term touchstone for Indian nationalism, framed as the ‘First War of Independence’ by later leaders.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Sustained explanation of two effects with precise examples and dates.
Secure: Clear explanation of two effects with relevant examples.
Developing: Two effects identified but uneven explanation.
Emerging: Brief identification only.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of Warren Hastings for the East India Company.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• At the time: as first Governor-General from 1772, Hastings centralised Company government and standardised tax collection.
• At the time: he expanded and reorganised the sepoy army that would later conquer the rest of India.
• At the time: he commissioned scholarly translation of Indian texts (Bhagavad Gita) and respected local elites — an early orientalist style of empire.
• Over time: his impeachment trial (1788-95) prompted Pitt’s India Act 1784 and parliamentary oversight of the Company.
• Over time: his governorship became the model the Company built on for the next 70 years.
• Limitation: his methods were ruthless — corruption charges were not entirely without basis.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Sustained significance covering both at the time and over time with precise dates and examples.
Secure: Clear significance with relevant examples.
Developing: Significance attempted but uneven.
Emerging: Brief identification only.

practice_questions.text: Explain how the social, cultural and economic impact of empire on India differed from its impact on Britain.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Economic in India: cash-crop economies replaced subsistence farming; British policy restricted Indian textile manufacturing to protect Lancashire mills; Bengal famines of 1770 and 1943 were worsened by colonial decisions.
• Economic in Britain: Indian tea, cotton and indigo fed the consumer revolution; Indian wealth funded country houses, banks and the Bank of England.
• Cultural in India: English-language schooling (Macaulay 1835) created a small Anglicised middle class; missionary activity was contested.
• Cultural in Britain: Indian words (bungalow, pyjamas, shampoo) entered English; Indian textiles, food and design influenced Victorian taste.
• Social in India: traditional power structures were disrupted; the Indian princely states retained influence but lost foreign-policy autonomy.
• Social in Britain: the Company offered a route to wealth for younger sons of the gentry, reshaping social mobility.
• Causal chain: empire was not symmetrical — Britain extracted wealth and exported manufactures, India received infrastructure but lost economic independence.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Sustained causal development comparing impact in both countries with precise examples.
Secure: Clear development with relevant examples.
Developing: Some development; balance uneven.
Emerging: Lists effects without explanation.
