lessons.title: The Scramble for Africa & the Boer War

before.content_html:
From Trade to Conquest, 1800-1914

In 1800, European powers controlled around 10% of Africa — mostly coastal forts for the slave trade and a few Cape settlements. By 1914, they controlled 90% of the continent. Britain ruled Egypt, the Sudan, Kenya, Uganda, Nigeria, the Gold Coast, Sierra Leone, the Cape, Natal, the Transvaal, the Orange Free State, Rhodesia and Nyasaland. The Scramble for Africa was driven by economic resources, ideas, and the personal ambitions of empire-builders — among them Cecil Rhodes, who summed up the era’s confidence with the line ‘I would annex the planets if I could.’

Key Fact

The Berlin Conference of 1884-85, chaired by Bismarck of Germany, set rules for European partition of Africa. No African leaders were present. The conference established that any power claiming African territory had to demonstrate ‘effective occupation’ — sparking a rush to plant flags and sign treaties with African chiefs.

Trade, Missionaries and the Anti-Slavery Cause

The earlier 19th century saw three British presences in Africa expand alongside each other. Trade: West African palm oil (used for soap and lubrication) replaced the slave trade as the main British export from the region. Missionaries: figures such as David Livingstone (active 1841-73) combined exploration with Christian conversion and anti-slavery campaigning. The Royal Navy West Africa Squadron: from 1808 it patrolled to suppress the Atlantic slave trade. These three strands gave Britain a moral self-image — the ‘civilising mission’ — that justified later territorial seizure. Critics at the time, and historians since, have pointed out that the same mission delivered profit to British exporters and political control to British administrators.

Egypt and the Sudan, 1882-1898

The opening of the Suez Canal in 1869 made Egypt strategically vital to Britain’s route to India. When Egyptian financial collapse and the Arabi Revolt threatened British investments and the canal in 1882, Gladstone (despite his reputation as an anti-imperialist) ordered the bombardment of Alexandria and a military occupation. Officially temporary, the occupation lasted 70 years. Sudanese resistance under the Mahdi killed General Gordon at Khartoum in 1885, and was eventually crushed by Kitchener at Omdurman in 1898 — a battle in which Maxim machine guns destroyed Mahdist cavalry, killing around 10,000 in a few hours.

Rhodes arrived in Cape Colony as a teenager in 1870, made his fortune in the Kimberley diamond fields and by 1888 controlled De Beers, which still mines most of the world’s diamonds today. As Cape Colony Prime Minister from 1890, he pushed the British South Africa Company north into present-day Zimbabwe and Zambia — territories that took his name (Rhodesia, until 1980). His ‘Cape to Cairo’ ambition was a continuous British strip of railway, telegraph and rule from southern to northern Africa. The 1895 Jameson Raid — an attempt to overthrow the Transvaal government — was a Rhodes-backed disaster that helped trigger the Boer War.

The Second Boer War, 1899-1902

Tensions between the British Cape Colony and the Boer republics (Transvaal and Orange Free State) erupted into war in October 1899. The Boers were Afrikaans-speaking descendants of Dutch settlers; the war was over gold (discovered on the Witwatersrand in 1886), the political rights of British settlers in the Transvaal, and rival imperial ambitions. The Boers’ early successes — the sieges of Mafeking, Kimberley and Ladysmith — humiliated Britain. By mid-1900 a much larger British force had captured Pretoria, but Boer commandos kept fighting a guerrilla war for two more years.

Britain responded by burning Boer farms and corralling civilians into concentration camps. Conditions were horrific: poor food, contaminated water, no medical care. Around 28,000 Boers (mostly children) died of disease, and at least 20,000 Africans died in separate camps held in even worse conditions. Emily Hobhouse’s 1901 visit and the Fawcett Commission report exposed the camps in Britain. The war ended in May 1902 with the Treaty of Vereeniging: the Boer republics joined the British Empire but with their language and culture protected. The cost in lives, money and reputation made many in Britain question the moral case for empire.

Imperial Propaganda and Social Darwinism

Empire was sold to the British public through a vast propaganda industry. Cigarette cards, music hall songs, Boys’ Own Paper, Girls’ Own Paper, Mr Bovril, the 1924 Empire Exhibition at Wembley, school textbooks — all told one story: empire was good for both ruler and ruled. The intellectual scaffolding for this was social Darwinism: the misuse of Darwin’s 1859 theory of evolution to argue that ‘fitter’ races would inevitably rule ‘weaker’ ones. This was bad biology — Darwin himself rejected the idea — but politically convenient. Rudyard Kipling’s 1899 poem ‘The White Man’s Burden’ framed empire as a moral duty to ‘civilise’.

Key Fact

The Second Boer War (1899-1902) cost Britain 22,000 dead, £200 million and damaged its imperial reputation. The use of concentration camps killed around 28,000 Boer civilians and at least 20,000 Africans. Emily Hobhouse’s exposure of the camps was a turning point in British public opinion about empire.

Linking to the Factor Essay

The Scramble for Africa is the test case for ideas as a factor in empire. Without social Darwinism, the ‘civilising mission’ and the propaganda that sold them, the political support for African expansion would have been thinner. Economic resources drove the practicalities — gold, diamonds, palm oil, cotton, rubber. The role of individuals was visible everywhere: Rhodes in southern Africa, Lugard in Nigeria, Kitchener in Sudan, the Mahdi and Cetshwayo on the African side. A 16-mark factor essay on Africa needs to weigh ideas against economic resources, and the strongest answers note that they reinforced each other — ideas justified what economic resources made profitable.

• Over time: Boer political memory shaped 20th-century South African nationalism and the route to apartheid in 1948.

lessons.title: Irish & Jewish Migration; Movement Within the Empire

before.content_html:
A Century of Mass Movement, 1815-1914

Between the end of the Napoleonic Wars (1815) and the start of the First World War (1914), Britain and its empire saw the largest movement of people in their history up to that point. Three flows define the period: Irish migrants pushed into Britain by famine and poverty, Jewish refugees pushed out of the Russian Empire by pogroms, and a vast traffic of Indians, Chinese and others across the empire as labour, often under indentured contracts. The British state also continued to push convicts out, sending around 162,000 people to Australia under transportation until 1868. None of these movements happened in isolation — they fed each other.

Key Fact

The Great Famine of 1845-49 killed around one million people in Ireland and pushed another one million to Britain. Russian pogroms from 1881 brought around 150,000 Jewish refugees to Britain by 1914. The 1905 Aliens Act — Britain’s first peacetime immigration law — was a direct response to that arrival.

Irish Migration: Push, Pull and the Famine

Irish migration to Britain pre-dates the famine: Liverpool already had a large Irish-Catholic community by the 1830s, working in dockyards, building canals and railways. The Great Famine of 1845-49 turned a steady migration into a crisis. The potato blight (a fungal disease) destroyed the staple crop of around three million Irish people; British government relief was slow, ideologically constrained by free-trade doctrine, and partial. Around one million Irish died; another million crossed to Britain or beyond.

The Irish settled in industrial cities — Liverpool, Manchester, Glasgow, London, Cardiff. By 1851 around 23% of Liverpool’s population was Irish-born; in Manchester it was around 13%. They lived in the worst housing, took the worst-paid manual jobs, and faced anti-Catholic and anti-Irish hostility — cartoons in Punch portrayed Irish migrants as ape-like, the ‘Paddy and the pig’ stereotype. Yet they kept communities alive: Catholic parish churches, Gaelic Athletic Association teams (founded 1884), and the political pressure that helped pass Catholic Emancipation (1829) and shaped Liberal politics for the rest of the century. Cardinal Newman’s 1851 conversion and the 1850 restoration of the Catholic hierarchy in England both responded to this Irish-Catholic presence.

Foreign immigration was a small fraction of the migration story. Far larger was the rural-to-urban shift inside Britain itself. In 1801 around 80% of the British population lived in the countryside; by 1901 around 80% lived in towns and cities. Manchester grew from 75,000 in 1801 to around 645,000 in 1901; Glasgow from 77,000 to 762,000. Cotton mills, steel works, mines and railways pulled rural workers off the land just as the Highland Clearances (Lesson 8) and similar enclosures pushed them. Irish, Jewish and (later) Caribbean migrants arrived into communities already in flux.

Jewish Migration: Pogroms, the East End and the Aliens Act

In 1881 Tsar Alexander II of Russia was assassinated. Across the Russian Empire, anti-Jewish riots — pogroms — killed thousands and dispossessed hundreds of thousands. The May Laws of 1882 imposed strict residential and economic restrictions on Russian Jews. Around two million Jews left the Russian Empire between 1881 and 1914; most went to the United States, but around 150,000 settled in Britain.

They concentrated in London’s East End — Whitechapel, Spitalfields, Stepney — and in Leeds, Manchester, Glasgow and South Shields. Jewish migrants worked in the ‘sweated trades’ (clothing, cabinetmaking, tailoring); ran small shops and printing presses; and built communal institutions including synagogues, the Jewish Chronicle (founded 1841), the Jewish Free School and Yiddish theatre. The 1905 Aliens Act, passed under pressure from Conservative MPs and groups like the British Brothers League, was the first peacetime restriction on immigration to Britain. It targeted ‘undesirable’ aliens — without naming Jews, but everyone understood whom it meant.

Transportation: Migration as Punishment

From 1788 the British state shipped convicts to Australia, in lieu of the prisons it did not have, and in lieu of the American colonies that had accepted convicts before 1776. Around 162,000 men, women and children were transported to New South Wales, Tasmania and Western Australia between 1788 and 1868. Most were sentenced for petty theft — one in three for stealing food or clothing — and around 20% were Irish, including political prisoners after the 1798 Rising and the 1848 Young Ireland uprising. Survivors’ descendants now number around 20% of the modern Australian population.

Asians in Africa: Indenture After Abolition

When slavery was abolished in 1833, plantations across the British Empire faced a labour crisis. Indenture filled the gap. Between 1834 and 1920, around 1.5 million Indians and 200,000 Chinese were shipped to British, French and Dutch colonies on three- to five-year contracts. Around 32,000 were sent to British East Africa to build the Uganda Railway (1896-1901), nicknamed the ‘Lunatic Express’ for its cost and danger. About 2,500 died. Around 6,500 stayed on after their contracts ended — the basis of the East African Asian community whose later expulsion by Idi Amin (Lesson 13) brought 27,200 Ugandan Asians to Britain in 1972.

Indenture was technically free contract labour, but conditions, mortality and physical control made many contemporaries call it ‘a new system of slavery’ (the title of Hugh Tinker’s 1974 history). Migrants did not always go home: around half of Indian indentured labourers stayed in their destination colonies, creating Indian communities from Mauritius to Trinidad to Fiji, and small but enduring populations in East and Southern Africa. The 4-mark comparison question can compare indenture with earlier slavery, with European emigration, or with later post-1948 Commonwealth migration. The strongest comparisons name dates, numbers and conditions.

Key Fact

Three nineteenth-century migrations show three different drivers. Irish migration was pushed by famine and economic collapse; Jewish migration was pushed by religious persecution; Asian movement within the empire was pulled by post-1833 plantation and infrastructure labour shortages. The 1905 Aliens Act was the British state’s first peacetime restriction on incoming migration.
before.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The 1845-49 Great Famine pushed around one million Irish to Britain; by 1851 nearly a quarter of Liverpool was Irish-born and Catholic Emancipation, the GAA and the restored Catholic hierarchy followed.
  • Russian pogroms from 1881 brought around 150,000 Jewish refugees to the East End and other industrial cities; the 1905 Aliens Act was the first peacetime British immigration restriction.
  • Empire migration ran in many directions: 162,000 convicts transported to Australia, 1.5 million Indian indentured labourers shipped across the empire, and the East African Asian community built by Uganda Railway workers and traders.

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways in which Irish migration to Britain in the 1840s and Jewish migration to Britain after 1881 were similar or different.
practice_questions.type: 4 marks — Two Ways Similar or Different
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Difference: Irish migration was pushed by economic collapse and famine; Jewish migration was pushed by religious persecution and pogroms in the Russian Empire.
• Difference: there was no legal restriction on Irish entry to Britain (it was internal Union movement); the Jewish arrivals provoked the 1905 Aliens Act, the first peacetime British immigration restriction.
• Similarity: both groups concentrated in industrial cities — Liverpool and Manchester for the Irish, the East End of London and Leeds for the Jewish migrants.
• Similarity: both faced hostile stereotyping in the British press — the Punch ‘Paddy and the pig’ cartoons for the Irish, the British Brothers League agitation for the Jewish arrivals.

[4 marks — 2 marks per comparison: 1 for a basic point, 2 for a developed point]

Secure: Two clear comparisons.
Developing: One developed; second basic.

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways in which transportation of British convicts to Australia and Indian indentured migration to East Africa were similar or different.
practice_questions.type: 4 marks — Two Ways Similar or Different
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Difference: transportation was a judicial punishment imposed by British courts on around 162,000 convicts (1788-1868); Indian indenture was a contract system used to recruit around 1.5 million workers across the empire (1834-1920).
• Difference: transportees had no legal right of return; indentured workers had a contract that in theory entitled them to a passage home after three to five years.
• Similarity: both moved labour around the empire under conditions of physical control — convict ships, indentured ships and plantation barracks shared many features.
• Similarity: both produced lasting communities at the destination: around 20% of modern Australians descend from convicts; East African Asian communities trace back to the Uganda Railway and indentured plantation labour.

practice_questions.marks:

• At the time: by 1851 around 23% of Liverpool’s population was Irish-born; Catholic emancipation (1829) and the 1850 restoration of the Catholic hierarchy responded to this presence.
• Over time: Irish migration shaped Liberal politics throughout the 19th century, with Gladstone’s Home Rule campaigns of 1886 and 1893 a direct response to the Irish vote in Britain.
• Over time: Irish-Catholic communities created lasting institutions — parishes, GAA clubs, Catholic schools — that defined British urban culture into the 20th century.
• Over time: the famine memory shaped Anglo-Irish relations through partition (1921), the Troubles and the modern republic.
• Limitation: integration over generations means present-day Irish-British identity is hard to track; the demographic story is clearer than the cultural one.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of the 1905 Aliens Act for British attitudes towards immigration.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• At the time: first peacetime restriction on immigration to Britain; targeted ‘undesirable’ aliens, primarily the Jewish refugees from the Russian Empire arriving since 1881.
• At the time: created an immigration officer system at the ports and an appeals process for those refused entry.
• At the time: gave political legitimacy to anti-immigration arguments, with figures like William Evans-Gordon and the British Brothers League shaping the debate.
• Over time: established the principle that the British state could choose whom to admit — a precedent for the 1914 Aliens Restriction Act, the 1962 Commonwealth Immigrants Act and modern immigration law.
• Over time: Jewish refugees from the 1930s, especially those fleeing Nazi Germany, faced barriers shaped in part by 1905 procedures and culture.
• Limitation: the 1905 Act admitted only around 1,000 refusals a year initially; its symbolic and legal importance was greater than its immediate numerical impact.

lessons.title: The End of Empire: Wars, Suez & Independence

before.content_html:
From World Power to Post-Imperial Power, 1914-1965

In 1914 Britain ruled around a quarter of the world’s population. By 1965 it ruled almost none of it. The First and Second World Wars, the rise of nationalist movements led by figures such as Mahatma Gandhi, Kwame Nkrumah and Jomo Kenyatta, and the diplomatic humiliation of the 1956 Suez Crisis combined to end the largest empire in modern history. For a 16-mark factor essay, this is the textbook test of how war, ideas (especially anti-colonial nationalism) and the role of individuals interacted with each other — rarely working alone.

Key Fact

India and Pakistan became independent on 14-15 August 1947 (around 12 million people displaced and at least one million killed in partition violence). Ghana became the first sub-Saharan African colony to gain independence on 6 March 1957. The 1956 Suez Crisis exposed Britain as no longer able to act independently of the United States.

The First World War: Promises and Mobilisation

The First World War mobilised the empire on a scale never seen before. Around 1.5 million Indian troops served, more than 600,000 in combat. About 200,000 from Africa fought, and West Indies Regiment troops served on the Western Front. They returned home expecting recognition and reform. Britain’s 1917 Montagu Declaration promised Indians ‘the gradual development of self-governing institutions’. The 1919 Government of India Act delivered limited reform; the same year, the Amritsar Massacre killed at least 379 unarmed Indians at a Sikh festival, exposing the gap between promise and reality. Mahatma Gandhi’s Indian National Congress mass campaigns — non-cooperation (1920-22), the Salt March (1930), Quit India (1942) — built on the resulting anger.

The Second World War: The Decisive Blow

The Second World War broke imperial Britain economically, militarily and morally. Around 2.5 million Indians served, the largest volunteer army in history; West African and East African forces fought in Burma and Italy; West Indian aircrew flew with the RAF. The 1942 fall of Singapore to Japan — in which 80,000 British, Indian and Australian soldiers surrendered — permanently shattered the myth of European racial superiority in Asia. The 1943 Bengal famine killed at least three million Indians; Churchill’s government diverted food to British troops. By 1945 Britain owed the United States the equivalent of around four years of national income, was rationing food at home, and had a Labour government committed to the welfare state. There was no money, no army and no will to maintain empire by force.

Attlee’s Labour government sent Lord Mountbatten as the last Viceroy in 1947. Boundary lines drawn by Cyril Radcliffe in five weeks divided Bengal and Punjab between India and Pakistan. Around 12 million people moved across the new borders; at least one million died in inter-communal violence. Gandhi opposed partition and was assassinated in January 1948 by a Hindu nationalist who saw him as too friendly to Muslims. Independence ended British rule over the ‘jewel in the crown’ — the empire’s biggest asset and the colony around which all imperial strategy had been built since the 1857 Rebellion (Lesson 9).

Suez 1956: The Public Humiliation

In July 1956 Egypt’s president Gamal Abdel Nasser nationalised the Suez Canal — British- and French-owned since 1869, the lifeline to the remaining empire. Anthony Eden conspired with France and Israel to retake the canal: Israel invaded the Sinai on 29 October; Britain and France issued an ultimatum and bombed Egyptian airfields on 31 October. Within ten days, US President Eisenhower ordered Britain to withdraw. The pound came under such pressure that the Treasury could not defend it without American help — help Eisenhower withheld until British troops left. The Suez Crisis ended Eden’s career and made it explicit: Britain could no longer act as a great imperial power without American consent. Decolonisation accelerated.

Africa: The Wind of Change

Kwame Nkrumah founded the Convention People’s Party in 1949 and used a programme of strikes and ‘positive action’ to make the Gold Coast ungovernable. Independent Ghana followed in 1957. Harold Macmillan’s 1960 ‘Wind of Change’ speech in Cape Town acknowledged that African nationalism would not be stopped. Nigeria became independent in 1960; Sierra Leone and Tanganyika in 1961; Uganda in 1962; Kenya in 1963 under Jomo Kenyatta.

Kenya’s path was the most violent. The 1952-1960 Mau Mau Emergency saw a Kikuyu insurgency against settler land-grabs and forced labour. The British response was extraordinary in its violence: at least 1.5 million Kenyans were detained or held in fortified villages; around 11,000 Mau Mau fighters were killed (some estimates run higher). Caroline Elkins’s 2005 book Britain’s Gulag exposed routine torture and unlawful killings in the camps. In 2013 the British government paid £19.9 million in compensation to 5,228 surviving detainees and apologised — an admission of state crime that the empire had denied for half a century.

Gandhi did not invent Indian nationalism — the Indian National Congress was founded in 1885 — but he transformed it. After his return from South Africa in 1915, he developed satyagraha (non-violent resistance) into a mass political technique. The 1930 Salt March, in which 78 followers walked 240 miles to make salt from seawater in defiance of the British monopoly, made the British Empire look ridiculous on world cinema screens. Gandhi’s influence reached far beyond India: Martin Luther King studied his methods, and Nkrumah’s ‘positive action’ in the Gold Coast was modelled on Gandhi’s.

Key Fact

The end of empire was not a single event but a process from 1945 to 1965. Britain’s post-1945 economic exhaustion, the Suez 1956 humiliation, and the leadership of Gandhi (India 1947), Nkrumah (Ghana 1957) and Kenyatta (Kenya 1963) combined to dismantle most of the empire in around 20 years.

practice_questions.text: ‘War was the main factor in the end of the British Empire after 1945.’ To what extent do you agree? Explain your answer with reference to war and other factors.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• War (in support): the Second World War left Britain bankrupt, owing the US the equivalent of around four years of national income; rationing continued at home until 1954.
• War (in support): the 1942 fall of Singapore to Japan shattered the myth of European racial superiority in Asia, fuelling post-war independence movements.
• War (in support): the 1956 Suez Crisis showed Britain could not act militarily without US consent; decolonisation accelerated immediately afterwards.
• Ideas: anti-colonial nationalism — Gandhi’s satyagraha, Nkrumah’s positive action, Pan-Africanism — gave colonised people a programme and an identity.
• Role of individuals: Gandhi (1947 Indian independence), Nkrumah (1957 Ghana), Kenyatta (1963 Kenya), Macmillan (1960 Wind of Change) — key figures shaped the timing and form of decolonisation.
• Government: the 1945 Labour government’s welfare-state priorities and 1947 Indian independence Act; the 1957 Macmillan government’s acceptance of African independence.
• Economic resources: the post-war dollar gap and the financial crisis at Suez 1956 made empire unaffordable.
• Top-band judgement: war was decisive in creating the conditions (1945 bankruptcy, 1956 humiliation), but ideas and individuals shaped what filled the vacuum. The factors reinforced each other — nationalism existed before 1939, but the wars made imperial defence economically and politically impossible.

[16 marks + 4 SPaG]

Secure: Clear argument addressing the named factor and at least one other, reaching a judgement.

lessons.title: Windrush, Commonwealth Migration & the Legacy of Empire

before.content_html:
Windrush 1948: Symbol, Not Beginning

On 22 June 1948 the troopship HMT Empire Windrush docked at Tilbury with 492 Caribbean migrants on board. The arrival is often called the start of multicultural Britain. It was nothing of the sort. People of African descent had lived in Britain since the Roman period; the 18th century saw a community of around 10,000-15,000 (Lesson 6); thousands of Caribbean and African seamen had served in the merchant marine and the World Wars. What made Windrush different was scale and timing. The 1948 British Nationality Act, passed three weeks before the ship docked, made every Commonwealth citizen a citizen of the United Kingdom and Colonies. Britain needed labour for post-war reconstruction. The Caribbean had unemployment. The combination produced the largest peacetime migration in modern British history.

Key Fact

HMT Empire Windrush docked at Tilbury on 22 June 1948 with 492 Caribbean migrants. The 1948 British Nationality Act, passed earlier that year, made every Commonwealth citizen a citizen of the United Kingdom and Colonies, opening the door to large-scale post-war migration.

Settling, Working, Resisting

Between 1948 and 1962 around 250,000 Caribbean migrants came to Britain, joined by smaller numbers of Indians, Pakistanis and West Africans. They worked in the National Health Service (founded the same week Windrush docked), London Transport, British Rail and the textile mills of Yorkshire and Lancashire. Recruitment was direct: London Transport had recruitment offices in Barbados from 1956; Enoch Powell, as Minister of Health, oversaw NHS recruitment from the Caribbean.

Reception was hostile. ‘No Irish, No Blacks, No Dogs’ signs appeared in boarding-house windows. Estate agents refused service. The 1958 Notting Hill riots saw white ‘Teddy Boy’ mobs attacking Caribbean residents over five nights; one of the largest gatherings reached around 700 people. The next year, the racist murder of Antiguan carpenter Kelso Cochrane went unsolved — a turning point in Caribbean political organisation in Britain.

Claudia Jones and the Carnival

Claudia Jones had been deported from the United States for Communist activities in 1955 and arrived in London via Trinidad. In response to the Notting Hill attacks she founded the West Indian Gazette (1958), Britain’s first major Black newspaper. In January 1959 she organised an indoor Caribbean carnival at St Pancras Town Hall, broadcast by the BBC. After her death in 1964 the carnival moved outdoors to Notting Hill itself; today the Notting Hill Carnival is the largest street festival in Europe and the most visible legacy of post-Windrush migration. Jones’s achievement is the textbook answer to a 16-mark essay question on the ‘role of individuals’ in shaping post-war Britain — she did not wait for British institutions, she built her own.

Indian and Pakistani migration was smaller than Caribbean migration in the 1950s but grew rapidly in the 1960s. The 1962 Commonwealth Immigrants Act — the first restriction on Commonwealth migration — produced a beat-the-ban surge that brought hundreds of thousands of Indians and Pakistanis to Britain before the door closed. They settled in textile-mill Yorkshire and Lancashire, in the Black Country, and in east London. The 1971 Immigration Act tightened restrictions further. By 1971 around 1.4 million Commonwealth-born residents lived in Britain; their British-born children would shape every aspect of British culture from Punjabi pop music to British curry to British politics.

Idi Amin and the Ugandan Asians, 1972

In August 1972 Ugandan dictator Idi Amin announced the expulsion of the country’s Asian community — around 80,000 people, most of them descendants of the Indian indentured workers and traders covered in Lesson 11. Amin gave them 90 days to leave, accusing them of ‘sabotaging the economy’. Around 27,200 came to Britain — the largest single arrival of refugees since the Huguenots almost three centuries earlier. The Heath government accepted them despite domestic opposition; the Uganda Resettlement Board ran a network of reception camps. Within ten years many had become entrepreneurs and shopkeepers in towns such as Leicester — one of Britain’s clearest examples of refugee migrants becoming an economic asset.

The Commonwealth and the Legacy of Empire

As the empire ended, the Commonwealth replaced it. Originally a club of white-settler dominions (1931), it was redefined in 1949 to allow republics — opening it to newly independent India and later the African states. By the 1970s the Commonwealth was a multi-racial institution headed by the Queen, with a Secretariat in London (founded 1965). It anchored British migration policy: Commonwealth citizens had been the basis of the 1948 Act, and successive immigration restrictions in 1962, 1968 and 1971 progressively narrowed Commonwealth citizenship rights without abolishing them.

The August-September 1958 attacks in Notting Hill ran for five nights. White ‘Teddy Boy’ mobs — one estimated at around 700 people — threw petrol bombs and chased Caribbean residents off the streets. The fascist Union Movement, led by Oswald Mosley, tried to capitalise on the unrest. The following May, Antiguan-born carpenter Kelso Cochrane was stabbed to death walking home from hospital after treating a broken thumb. The murder was never solved, but the funeral procession of 1,200 mourners showed a Caribbean community organising politically. The 1958 attacks and the Cochrane case shaped Black British activism for decades — from Claudia Jones’s carnival to the 1981 Brixton Riots and the 1993 murder of Stephen Lawrence.

In 1982 Britain went to war over the Falkland Islands, a sparsely populated South Atlantic archipelago invaded by Argentina. Margaret Thatcher dispatched a naval task force; 255 British and 649 Argentinian servicemen died before Argentina’s surrender on 14 June 1982. The Falklands War was the last expeditionary war of the post-imperial era. It revived a kind of patriotic sentiment that the post-Suez generation had thought impossible — and it confirmed the principle that the remaining British Overseas Territories were defended by their inhabitants’ choice rather than imperial possession.

Key Fact

The 1958 Notting Hill attacks led directly to Claudia Jones’s 1959 indoor Caribbean Carnival — ancestor of today’s Notting Hill Carnival. In 1972 Britain accepted 27,200 Ugandan Asians expelled by Idi Amin, the largest refugee arrival since the Huguenots.

The Windrush Scandal, 2018

In 2018 a series of Guardian reports revealed that members of the Windrush generation — people who had arrived as British subjects, lived legally in Britain for decades and never been issued papers — had been wrongly detained, denied healthcare, refused work, and in some cases deported to countries they had not seen since childhood. The 2017 destruction of landing-card archives by the Home Office had left them unable to prove their status. At least 164 people were wrongly removed; thousands more were illegally detained or denied benefits. The 2020 Windrush Lessons Learned Review described the scandal as the result of ‘institutional ignorance and thoughtlessness towards the issue of race’. Compensation has been slow: by 2024 fewer than half of valid claims had been resolved. The Windrush story therefore did not end in 1948 — it is a live political issue 75 years later.

lessons.title: Britain & Europe: From EEC to Brexit

before.content_html:
From Empire to Europe, 1945-2020

As Britain dismantled its empire (Lesson 12), it had to decide what kind of country it would be next. Three answers were offered. The first was the United States: post-war Britain leaned heavily on the ‘special relationship’. The second was the Commonwealth (Lesson 13). The third — for most of the period covered here — was Europe. Britain joined the EEC in 1973, voted to remain in 1975, voted to leave the European Union in 2016 and finally departed on 31 January 2020. Across that 47-year membership, around 5 million Europeans came to live in Britain — the largest sustained inflow in modern British history. The Brexit debate was, more than anything else, a debate about that migration.

Key Fact

Britain joined the EEC on 1 January 1973 under Edward Heath. A 1975 referendum voted 67% to remain. The 23 June 2016 referendum voted 52% to leave the European Union; Britain formally left on 31 January 2020.

Reconstruction and the Marshall Plan

The Second World War left Britain bankrupt. The 1945 Anglo-American loan and the 1948 Marshall Plan gave Britain $2.7 billion in US aid — more than any other European country — on condition of free-trade reform and a commitment to European reconstruction. The Attlee government built the welfare state out of these funds: the NHS opened on 5 July 1948, three weeks before the Empire Windrush docked. Rationing, however, continued until 1954. By the time France, West Germany, Italy and the Benelux countries founded the EEC in 1957, Britain had chosen to stay outside — preferring to bet on the Commonwealth and the ‘special relationship’.

In Twice, Out Once: Britain’s European Path 1961-1975

By 1961 it was clear that the EEC was outperforming Britain economically. Macmillan applied for membership; Charles de Gaulle vetoed Britain’s application twice (1963, 1967), distrusting British loyalty to the United States. Heath finally negotiated entry in 1972, and Britain joined on 1 January 1973. The Wilson Labour government held a confirmatory referendum in 1975. The choice was ‘Yes’ or ‘No’ on staying in. The campaign cut across party lines — Wilson’s Cabinet split — and produced a 67% to 33% vote to remain.

The EEC was always a product of the Cold War. It tied Western Europe together politically and economically, with NATO providing the military shield. The 1989-1990 fall of the Berlin Wall and the collapse of the Soviet Union changed the strategic logic. The 1992 Maastricht Treaty turned the EEC into the European Union, with deeper political integration, a single currency project (which Britain opted out of in 1992), and a new commitment to enlargement eastward. The 2004 enlargement — ten new member states, mainly post-Communist Eastern Europe — was a Cold-War-ending project that would later become a Brexit issue.

2004 A8 Migration: Free Movement and the British Choice

In 2004 the EU admitted ten new countries: Poland, Czech Republic, Slovakia, Hungary, Slovenia, Estonia, Latvia, Lithuania, Malta and Cyprus. EU treaties allowed older member states to apply transitional restrictions on free movement of workers from the eight Eastern European entrants (the ‘A8’). Most older members imposed seven-year limits. Britain, Ireland and Sweden chose not to. The Blair government’s estimate was that around 13,000 East Europeans a year would come.

The actual number was vastly larger. Between 2004 and 2014 around one million Polish citizens settled in Britain, plus large numbers of Lithuanians, Romanians (after 2007), Bulgarians and Hungarians. By the 2011 census, Polish was the second most-spoken language in England after English, and Polish-born residents were the largest non-UK-born group in Britain. The migration was concentrated in agriculture, hospitality, construction, transport and food processing — sectors which had become structurally dependent on East European labour by the time of the 2016 referendum.

Brexit, 2016-2020

David Cameron called the Brexit referendum to settle a long-running Conservative Party split. The 23 June 2016 vote went 52%-48% in favour of leaving. Migration was central to the Leave campaign — Vote Leave’s ‘Take Back Control’ slogan was understood, above all, as taking control of immigration. Polling consistently showed that immigration was the single most important issue for Leave voters. Britain formally left the EU on 31 January 2020 and ended free movement on 31 December 2020. New points-based rules treated EU and non-EU migrants alike on a salary and skills basis.

The actual effect on migration numbers was paradoxical. Net migration fell briefly during the pandemic but reached record highs of 906,000 in the year to mid-2023 — nearly double the level under free movement — driven by a global recruitment drive for the NHS and care sector and by visa schemes for Hong Kong British Nationals (Overseas) (over 192,000 by 2024) and for Ukrainians fleeing the 2022 Russian invasion. The Brexit migration debate had been less about numbers than about who got to set them.

European migration is only part of the story. Since 1990 Britain has received Somali, Iraqi, Kosovar, Afghan, Syrian and Ukrainian refugees from war zones; Hong Kongers under the BN(O) visa from 2021; Indian, Nigerian and Filipino health and care workers; Chinese students who account for nearly a quarter of international university enrolments. By 2023 around 14% of UK residents were born abroad — up from 8% in 2001 and 4% in 1951. The thematic study’s opening question — ‘how has Britain’s identity been shaped by interaction with the wider world?’ — reaches into present-day demographics in a way no previous chapter does.

Key Fact

The 2004 EU enlargement opened free movement to eight Eastern European countries. By 2011 around one million Polish citizens lived in Britain — the largest non-UK-born group. Free movement ended on 31 December 2020 after the 2016 Brexit referendum.
before.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Marshall aid (1948) anchored Britain to Western Europe; Britain joined the EEC in 1973 after two French vetoes and confirmed membership in the 1975 referendum.
  • The 2004 EU enlargement and Britain’s decision not to apply transitional restrictions brought around one million Polish citizens to Britain by 2011 — the largest non-UK-born group.
  • The 23 June 2016 referendum voted 52%-48% to leave; free movement ended 31 December 2020 but post-Brexit non-EU migration reached record levels by 2023.

• Over time: end of free movement on 31 December 2020 created acute labour shortages in those exact sectors, which the post-Brexit points-based system has only partly resolved.
• Limitation: the British state had legal authority to apply transitional restrictions but chose not to — the ‘significance’ here is partly a story of British political choices.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Sustained significance covering both at the time and over time with precise dates and examples.
Secure: Clear significance with relevant examples.
Developing: Significance attempted but uneven.
Emerging: Brief identification only.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of the 2016 Brexit referendum for British migration policy.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• At the time: 52%-48% Leave vote on 23 June 2016 mandated the end of free movement.
• At the time: politically toxic for the major parties — Cameron resigned, Labour split, the Conservative Party committed to delivery.
• Over time: 31 January 2020 formal withdrawal; 31 December 2020 end of free movement.
• Over time: post-Brexit points-based system treats EU and non-EU migrants alike on salary and skills criteria; the government chose to use it to recruit globally for the NHS and care sectors.
• Over time: net migration reached 906,000 in the year to mid-2023, nearly double the level under free movement — the political settlement turned out to be about who controls migration, not its scale.
• Over time: the Leave vote reshaped the structure of the United Kingdom itself — reviving Scottish independence debate and complicating the Northern Ireland Protocol.
• Limitation: the long-term economic significance is still being assessed; the political significance is already evident.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Sustained significance covering both at the time and over time with precise dates and examples.
Secure: Clear significance with relevant examples.
Developing: Significance attempted but uneven.
Emerging: Brief identification only.

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways in which migration from the European Union after 2004 was similar to or different from earlier Commonwealth migration after 1948.
practice_questions.type: 4 marks — Two Ways Similar or Different
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Difference: Commonwealth migration was based on shared British subjecthood under the 1948 Nationality Act; EU migration was based on free movement under EEC and EU treaties.
• Difference: Commonwealth migrants came from countries with deep British connections through empire; EU migrants from 2004 came from Eastern European countries with no shared imperial history.
• Similarity: both were direct results of British government decisions (1948 Nationality Act; 2004 decision not to apply transitional restrictions) and exceeded official forecasts.
• Similarity: both became politically contested when their scale produced a backlash — the 1962 Commonwealth Immigrants Act after Caribbean arrivals, the 2016 Brexit vote after Eastern European arrivals.

[4 marks — 2 marks per comparison: 1 for a basic point, 2 for a developed point]
Mastering: Two developed comparisons with precise dates and named events.
Secure: Two clear comparisons.
Developing: One developed; second basic.
Emerging: Vague generalisation.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of the end of the Cold War for Britain’s relationship with Europe.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• At the time: 1989 fall of the Berlin Wall and 1991 collapse of the Soviet Union ended the security logic that had bound Western Europe together since 1957.
• At the time: the 1992 Maastricht Treaty turned the EEC into the European Union, with deeper political integration; Britain opted out of the single currency.
• Over time: the 2004 EU enlargement absorbed eight post-Communist Eastern European countries, reshaping intra-EU migration.
• Over time: shaped the political environment for the 2016 Brexit referendum — migration debate was inseparable from EU enlargement debate.
• Over time: post-Cold-War European integration eventually became the issue Britain left the EU to escape.
• Limitation: the immediate post-1990 effect was modest — the major migration changes followed the 2004 enlargement, fifteen years later.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Sustained significance covering both at the time and over time with precise dates and examples.
Secure: Clear significance with relevant examples.
Developing: Significance attempted but uneven.
Emerging: Brief identification only.

before.exam_tip_html: For an 8-mark ‘Explain a Development’ question, the relationship between Britain and Europe is unusually rich material because the development is causal, not just chronological: each step shaped the next. Use this in your answer. Marshall aid (1948) shaped reconstruction; the Cold War (1945-89) shaped the EEC’s purpose; eastward enlargement (2004) reshaped UK migration; the migration debate shaped the Brexit vote (2016). Show consequences, not just sequence.
